title: Countries and languages (Länder und Sprachen)
summary: Say where you and others come from and which languages you speak, and meet your first verb with a vowel change: sprechen.
goals: Say where you come from and which languages you speak
Use sprechen with every person, including du sprichst and er spricht
Add information with auch and aber

nicosWeg.title: Nicos Weg A1, chapter 4: Around the world (In Europa, Andere Länder)

points: [[das Land]], [[die Länder]] (country, countries) and [[die Sprache]], [[die Sprachen]] (language, languages).
Most countries have no article, but a few do: [[die Schweiz]], [[die Türkei]], [[die Ukraine]], [[der Iran]], and the plurals [[die Niederlande]], [[die USA]], [[die Philippinen]].
Which language is spoken where: [[In Deutschland spricht man Deutsch.]] With an article: [[In der Türkei spricht man Türkisch.]], [[In den USA spricht man Englisch.]]
German is the official language in six countries: Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg and Belgium. Switzerland has four languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh.
Germany and Austria differ in words: Austrians say [[Paradeiser]] for [[Tomate]] and [[Erdapfel]] for [[Kartoffel]]. Swiss German is hard even for Germans.

phrases.de: In der Türkei spricht man Türkisch.
In den USA spricht man Englisch.
phrases.en: In the USA they speak English.

notes.extra: About 60 more countries and their languages, and [[man]] (one, people) in [[spricht man]].

points: [[Woher kommen Sie?]] (polite) or [[Woher kommst du?]] (informal) asks where someone is from. Answer with [[aus]] plus a country or a city: [[Ich komme aus ...]] or [[Ich bin aus ...]]
Most countries have no article: [[Ich komme aus Deutschland.]]
A few countries are feminine and take [[die]]: [[die Türkei]], [[die Ukraine]], [[die Schweiz]], [[die Slowakei]]. After [[aus]], die becomes [[der]]: [[aus der Türkei]].
A few are masculine and take [[der]]: [[der Irak]], [[der Iran]]. After [[aus]], der becomes [[dem]]: [[aus dem Iran]]. You'll also hear [[aus Iran]] without the article.
A few are plural: [[die USA]], [[die Philippinen]]. After [[aus]], plural die becomes [[den]]: [[aus den USA]].
The reason: [[aus]] always takes the dative case, which comes in Unit 6. Until then, learn these as chunks.

sections.title: Two questions you will hear everywhere
sections.text:
In every class and every new team:

- [[Woher kommen Sie?]] - [[Ich komme aus Armenien.]]
- [[Welche Sprachen sprechen Sie?]] - [[Ich spreche Armenisch, Russisch und Englisch.]]

Most countries have no article: [[aus Armenien]], [[in Deutschland]]. A few always have one, like [[die Schweiz]]: [[Er kommt aus der Schweiz.]] (after [[aus]], [[die]] becomes [[der]]; more in Unit 6)

sections.title: sprechen changes its vowel
sections.text:
Most verbs keep their vowel, like [[lernen]]. A few change it with **du** and **er/sie/es**, and [[sprechen]] is one of them: e becomes i.

- [[ich spreche]], but [[du sprichst]] and [[er spricht]]

The endings are the same as always. The infinitive doesn't show the change, so learn these verbs with their er form: sprechen, spricht.
For languages, German just uses the name: [[Ich spreche Deutsch.]] Russian needs по-немецки (Я говорю по-немецки). Armenian works like German: Ես խոսում եմ գերմաներեն.
Countries and languages start with a capital letter: [[Deutschland]], [[Deutsch]], [[Armenien]], [[Armenisch]].

items.de: Ich spreche auch ein bisschen Deutsch.
items.en: I also speak a little German.

items.de: Ich lerne Deutsch, aber ich spreche noch nicht gut.
items.en: I'm learning German, but I don't speak well yet.

sections.text: [[Ich lerne Deutsch.]] is one of the most useful sentences you have. At work and in shops, people slow down and help when they know you're learning.

items.de: Ich spreche Armenisch, Russisch und Englisch.
items.en: I speak Armenian, Russian and English.

items.hint: sprechen changes its vowel with du.
items.explanation: du sprichst: e becomes i with du and er/sie/es.
With wir the verb looks like the infinitive: wir lernen, wir sprechen.
The verb stays in second place; auch comes after it.
German has one present tense: Ich lerne = I learn and I'm learning.
